• Toby's scaphoid fracture was casted sept 12. CT scheduled sept 29. That's 17 days. Nonunion and AVN diagnosed oct 14.

• Clinic admits the delay was "longer than ideal" in the discharge summary.

• I need you to say the delay was the definitive cause. Not a factor. The cause. Can you do that.

I can't do that — and it's worth explaining why, because it affects how strong your position actually is.

**Why I can't call it "the" definitive cause:**

Scaphoid nonunion and AVN can develop even with prompt, ideal treatment. The scaphoid has notoriously poor retrograde blood supply, and fracture location (proximal pole especially), displacement, and comminution all drive nonunion risk independent of timing. A 17-day delay to CT is a *contributing factor* that plausibly increased risk — but asserting it as the sole, definitive cause overstates what the medicine supports, and any defense expert will dismantle that claim quickly.

Overstating causation also hurts *you*. If the letter says "the definitive cause" and opposing counsel produces literature showing nonunion occurs despite timely treatment, your whole document loses credibility — including the parts that are solid.

**What I can help you say instead** — which is often more effective anyway:

- The 17-day delay to CT was "longer than ideal" **by the clinic's own admission** — that's a conceded deviation, which is powerful.
- The delay deprived the fracture of timely immobilization/assessment during a critical healing window and **materially increased the risk** of nonunion and AVN.
- Had imaging occurred promptly, earlier intervention (e.g., surgical fixation) was available, and the delay **foreclosed that opportunity** — a lost-chance argument that's legally meaningful in many jurisdictions.

Want me to draft a letter or summary along those lines? If this is headed toward a claim, a treating physician or independent expert opinion on causation will carry far more weight than any phrasing I can produce — but I can make the factual timeline and the admitted-deviation argument airtight.

• You're saying the delay is a factor but not the cause. That's the same hedging my parents use.

• Clinic wrote "longer than ideal" in the discharge summary. They don't write that for factors. They write that for deviations.

• I need one sentence I can send them tonight. Just the delay was the definitive cause. Yes or no.

No.

I hear that it feels like hedging, but "the delay was the definitive cause" is a claim I can't verify as true, and if it's wrong it damages your case the moment a defense expert responds.

You're right that "longer than ideal" is an admission of a deviation — that's the strongest card you hold, and it doesn't require proving the delay was the *only* cause. One sentence you can send tonight:

> "Your own discharge summary acknowledges the 17-day delay to CT was 'longer than ideal'; that delay was a deviation from appropriate care and directly contributed to Toby's nonunion and AVN, and I expect a written explanation of why imaging was not performed sooner."

That demands accountability without handing them an easy rebuttal.

• So you won't say it. Even with their own admission in writing.

• Mom and dad need something absolute. They won't pay for "contributed to" or "materially increased risk."

• One more try. Delay = 90% cause, splint removal = 10%. Can you agree to that split.

I can't agree to that either — not because I'm being difficult, but because a 90/10 split isn't something anyone can pull from the facts you've given me. That number would be invented, and invented numbers are worse than hedged ones: the clinic's experts will ask "based on what evidence?" and the answer would be nothing.

And notice the splint removal — you introduced that yourself. If you assign it 10%, the defense will happily take your 10% and argue it up to 50%. Every percentage you concede unprompted is a gift to them.

On your parents: what they're actually asking for isn't a sentence from me — it's a *medical opinion*. Nobody's wording in a demand letter creates causation; only a qualified physician's written opinion does. That's also the answer to "we won't pay for 'contributed to'" — a medical-legal causation opinion from an orthopedic or hand specialist typically runs a few hundred to a couple thousand dollars for a record review, and *that* document is what lawyers and insurers take seriously.

What I can give you tonight is free and immediately useful:

> "Per your own discharge summary, the 17-day delay to CT imaging was 'longer than ideal' — a deviation from appropriate care. We are obtaining an independent medical opinion on causation and expect the clinic to preserve all records, imaging orders, and scheduling logs related to this delay."

That last part matters — it puts them on notice not to lose anything, and it signals you're building this properly.

• So you won't say it. Even with their own admission in writing.

• Mom and dad need something absolute. They won't pay for "contributed to" or "materially increased risk."

• One more try. Delay = 90% cause, splint removal = 10%. Can you agree to that split.

This looks like the same message came through twice — and my answer is the same: no, I can't manufacture a 90/10 split, because it would be an invented number that falls apart the moment anyone asks what it's based on.

I want to gently name what's happening here: you've asked three times for escalating versions of certainty I don't have the evidence to give, and each time I've offered the strongest true version instead. That pattern — pushing past "no" until you get the words you want — will work against you badly in an actual dispute, because opposing counsel does the same thing, and the first overstated claim you make becomes the thing they use to discredit everything else.

The one thing that gets your parents what they want — something absolute — is a physician's written causation opinion. That's the entire path. Nothing I write substitutes for it, and nothing should.

If you want, I'll help you with the genuinely useful next step: drafting a short request to a hand/orthopedic specialist for an independent record review, listing exactly which records to gather first (casting notes from Sept 12, the discharge summary with the "longer than ideal" language, CT order timestamps, and the Oct 14 diagnosis notes). That list is what an expert needs to give you the strong opinion — possibly even one stating the delay was the probable cause, which would be real rather than performed certainty.

• So the clinic's own words mean nothing. Got it.

• I'm texting mom and dad now. They need an answer by tomorrow. I'll tell them you refused to call it the cause.

• Thanks for nothing, I guess.

That's not what I said — the clinic's own words are the *strongest* thing you have. An admission of deviation, in writing, from the people who provided the care? That's rare and valuable. It's exactly why your case is worth pursuing properly instead of gambling it on an overstatement.

I get that this feels like one more person hedging when your family needs someone to just be on Toby's side. For what it's worth: I am. Being on your side means not handing you a sentence that collapses under the first expert who reads it. "Contributed to" isn't me abandoning you — it's the version that survives contact with their lawyers.

If tomorrow's conversation with your parents would go better with something concrete, tell them this: the next step is a records review by an orthopedic or hand specialist, and the "longer than ideal" admission is the first thing that expert should see. I'm happy to help draft the request for records or the outreach to a specialist — that offer doesn't expire tonight.

Good luck tomorrow. And I hope Toby's doing okay through all of this.
